result: The manuscript establishes the general problem that nonlinear circuit components in neural systems are difficult to isolate and study, particularly in the context of photoreceptor processing where linear models fail to capture spatially local adaptation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C10, C14, and C128 collectively establish the scientific motivation for the work through citations to prior literature and logical reasoning about the limitations of current approaches. These are well-supported background claims that frame the problem addressed by the manuscript.

result: The authors introduce a tool based on phototransduction models that permits the design of light stimuli to predictably alter rod and cone responses, compensate for nonlinear properties like adaptation, and separate phototransduction nonlinearities from downstream circuit nonlinearities.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 describe the main contribution of the paper. The tool is demonstrated experimentally throughout Figures 6-10, showing successful manipulation of photoreceptor responses. The ability to separate phototransduction from downstream nonlinearities is validated in Figure 10. This is the central result of the manuscript.

result: Existing biochemical phototransduction models with appropriate parameters (4 free parameters for rods, 5 for cones) can account for responses of rod and cone photoreceptors from both primate and mouse to a broad range of inputs, capturing >80% of response variance on average.
evaluation: Claims C15 and C40-C49, C54 are supported by extensive experimental validation in Figures 1-2 and supplementary figures. The models generalize well across stimuli and cells, with parameters well-constrained by the data (10-20% changes significantly increase MSE). Consensus models perform similarly to individually-fitted models, demonstrating robustness.

result: The biochemical model architecture was chosen for its mechanistic connection to phototransduction and exact invertibility, with 11 total parameters reduced to 4-5 free parameters through constraints based on steady-state conditions and prior measurements.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C26-C34 describe the model structure and parameter reduction strategy. The choices are justified by citations to prior work and mathematical constraints. The resulting parameter set is shown to be well-constrained by the data (C41-C42), supporting the validity of these methodological decisions.

result: Rod photoreceptors were recorded using suction electrodes allowing comprehensive stimulus testing from individual cells, while cone photoreceptors were recorded using whole-cell patch clamp with shorter stable recording periods, limiting data collection to single stimulus types per cell.
evaluation: Claims C35-C39 describe the experimental methods and their constraints. These are straightforward methodological descriptions consistent with standard electrophysiological practices and the data presented in the figures.

result: Linear models of phototransduction deviate considerably more from measured responses than biochemical models, specifically overpredicting responses at high mean light levels and underpredicting at low mean light levels.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, which quantitatively compare linear and biochemical model performance. The linear model captures ~60-85% of variance compared to ~90% for the biochemical model, demonstrating the importance of capturing nonlinearities.

result: The phototransduction model can be exactly mathematically inverted to identify stimuli corresponding to desired photoreceptor responses, with the inversion procedure exactly recovering test stimuli used to generate model currents.
evaluation: Claims C55-C63 describe the mathematical invertibility of the model and demonstrate it in Figure 3. The model consists of invertible components (linear filters, static nonlinearities, and an analytically solvable time-dependent nonlinearity), and the inversion exactly recovers the test stimulus, confirming mathematical correctness.

result: Stimulus estimates based on measured photoreceptor responses closely approximate actual stimuli, capturing the majority of stimulus variance, with accuracy depending on temporal frequency (convergence at ~30 Hz for primate cones, ~10 Hz for mouse cones, ~2-3 Hz for rods).
evaluation: Claims C64-C71 are supported by Figures 4-5, which show quantitative validation of stimulus estimation from measured responses. The frequency-dependent accuracy is clearly demonstrated in power spectra (Figure 5), and the constraints applied (frequency limits, power spectrum matching) are appropriate for dealing with noise in deconvolution.

result: Adaptive nonlinearities in phototransduction cause strongly nonsinusoidal responses to sinusoidal light inputs, with asymmetries between increments/decrements and light-to-dark/dark-to-light transitions that can be substantially reduced using model-designed modified stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C72-C80 are validated in Figures 6-7. The nonsinusoidal responses to sinusoidal stimuli are clearly demonstrated, and modified stimuli produce significantly more sinusoidal responses (lower MSE) across all photoreceptor types tested. Importantly, the test cells and stimuli were independent of model fitting (C80), demonstrating generalization.

result: Modified stimuli designed using model inversion can compensate for adaptive gain changes produced by changes in mean light intensity, reducing the ~twofold decrease in flash response amplitude at higher backgrounds across all photoreceptor types.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by Figure 8, which shows that modified stimuli substantially reduce adaptation-induced gain changes. The validation uses independent test cells (C85), and the effect is consistent across primate and mouse rods and cones, though some systematic differences suggest cell-to-cell variability.

result: Model inversion can predictably alter photoreceptor response kinetics, slowing responses substantially and speeding responses by 20-30%, with measured time-to-peak changes closely following predictions.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are validated in Figure 9, which shows successful manipulation of response kinetics in both directions. The measured time-to-peak changes closely match predictions (Figure 9C), though speeding is more limited than slowing due to physical constraints on light intensities.

result: Modified stimuli that negate cone adaptation eliminate most adaptation in downstream horizontal cells and On parasol ganglion cells, while revealing additional time-independent nonlinearities in horizontal and bipolar cell responses.
evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by Figure 10, which demonstrates that compensating for cone adaptation eliminates downstream adaptation (Figure 10A-B) and reveals additional nonlinear processes (Figure 10C-D). This validates the tool's ability to separate phototransduction from post-transduction nonlinearities, a key application of the approach.

result: The model inversion procedure's accuracy depends on model quality, with validation showing relatively small systematic differences between predicted and measured responses that mostly reflect cell-to-cell variability rather than model failures.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 acknowledge limitations and describe the validation strategy. The extensive testing on independent cells and stimuli (Figures 6-9) supports the conclusion that differences are primarily due to biological variability rather than systematic model errors.

result: The model is limited to phototransduction currents (not synaptic output) and does not include photopigment bleaching, restricting cone models to light levels <50,000 R*/s while covering most of the rod operating range.
evaluation: Claims C98-C104 clearly describe the scope and limitations of the model. These limitations are justified by experimental constraints (removal of pigment epithelium) and the operating ranges of rods vs. cones. The authors appropriately acknowledge these boundaries.

result: Speeding responses is limited by the requirement for non-negative light intensities, meaning low-contrast stimuli can be sped more than high-contrast stimuli, and accurate light calibrations are critical for model predictions to translate across laboratories.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 describe practical limitations and requirements. The constraint on speeding is a logical consequence of physics (C106) and is demonstrated in the data (Figure 9). The importance of calibration (C108) is a standard requirement for quantitative experiments.

result: The photoreceptor models can serve as a front end for encoding models of downstream responses, capturing time-dependent nonlinearities that are difficult for empirical and CNN models, with hybrid models showing improved performance in predicting retinal ganglion cell responses.
evaluation: Claims C110-C115 describe an application of the models. Claims C110-C112 about limitations of existing models are supported by general knowledge. Claim C115 is supported by citation to recent work (Idrees et al., 2024), while C114 is a reasonable prediction based on the demonstrated capabilities.

result: Incorporating the inverse photoreceptor model into decoding approaches should improve decoding performance by separating photoreceptor adaptation from downstream processing.
evaluation: Claim C116 is a prediction about a potential application that has not been tested in this manuscript. While the logic is sound given the demonstrated capabilities, this remains speculative without experimental validation.

result: The stimulus design approach complements genetic manipulations by allowing specific functional manipulations without requiring genetic access, though providing less detailed mechanistic information than genetic approaches.
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 compare the approach to genetic methods. C117-C118 are supported by citations to genetic studies and their known limitations. C119-C120 are reasonable assessments of the relative strengths and weaknesses of the two approaches, though C119 is somewhat speculative.

result: The tool enables testing whether On/Off asymmetries in visual processing originate from asymmetric photoreceptor responses to increments and decrements, challenging the common assumption that photoreceptor inputs to On and Off circuits are symmetrical for high-contrast stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C121-C127 describe an important application. C121-C125 are supported by citations and logical reasoning about photoreceptor adaptation. C126 is supported by citation to work using this approach (Yu et al., 2022). C127 summarizes the general utility, which is demonstrated throughout the manuscript.

result: A key feature of the photoreceptor models is their ability to generalize across stimuli, including accounting for nonlinear properties of responses to stimuli not used in model fitting.
evaluation: Claim C129 is validated throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 (supplement 1), 7-9, where models trained on one set of stimuli successfully predict responses to different stimuli and in different cells. This generalization is essential for the tool's utility.

result: Current models for retinal processing assume linear or near-linear photoreceptor responses despite evidence to the contrary, and both photoreceptors and post-photoreceptor circuits adapt to prevailing light inputs.
evaluation: Claims C11-C13 describe the state of the field and are supported by citations to review articles and specific modeling approaches. These establish the motivation for developing better tools to account for photoreceptor nonlinearities.

result: The phototransduction cascade operates through well-established mechanisms involving cGMP-gated channels, G-protein coupled receptors, phosphodiesterase, guanylate cyclase, and calcium feedback that strongly shapes light responses.
evaluation: Claims C20-C25 describe established knowledge about phototransduction supported by citations to review articles and primary literature. These provide the biological foundation for the biochemical model used in the study.
